parsing_res_list.block_content: For each pressure range there is a particle, or wind velocity associated with the blast wave that causes a dynamic pressure on objects in the path of the wave. In the free field, these dynamic pressures are essentially functions of the air density and particle velocity. For typical conditions, standard relationships have been established between the peak incident shock pressure $(P_{s o})$ , the peak dynamic pressure $(q_{o})$ ,the air particle velocity, and the air density behind the shock front. The magnitudes of the dynamic pressures, particle velocity and air density are solely a function of the peak incident shock pressure, and, therefore, independent of the explosion size. Figure 2-3 (+) gives the values of the parameters versus the peak incident shock pressure. Of the three parameters, the dynamic pressure is the most important for determining the loads on structures.

For design purposes, it is necessary to establish the variation or decay of both the incident shock and dynamic pressures with time since the effects on the structure subjected to a blast loading depend upon the full pressure history of the loading. The pressure history from the incident shock wave (Figure 2-190 (+)) is characterized by an abrupt rise in pressure to a peak value, a period of decay to ambient pressure, and a period in which the pressure drops below ambient (negative pressure phase).

The rate of decay of the incident shock pressure and dynamic pressure, after the passage of the shock front, is a function of the peak pressure (both positive and negative phases) and the size of the detonation. For design purposes, the actual shape of the pressure history may be approximated with an equivalent right triangular pressure pulse. The actual positive phase duration is replaced by a fictitious duration $t_{o t}$ that is expressed as a function of the total positive impulse i and peak pressure $P$ as shown in Equation 2-6.

The above relationship for the equivalent triangular pulse is applicable to the incident as well as the reflected shock pressures. However, in the case of the latter, the value of the pressure and impulse used with Equation 2-6 is equivalent to that associated with the reflected wave. The fictitious duration of the dynamic pressure may be assumed to be equal to that of the incident shock pressure.

A similar procedure is used to determine the pressure history for the negative phase of the blast load. The equivalent triangular pressure-time curve for the negative phase has a fictitious duration $t_{o f}$ given by Equation 2-7, where i and $p^{-}$ are the total impulse and the peak pressure, respectively, of the negative pulse of either the incident or reflected shock wave. The equivalent pressure history begins at zero after the positive phase has ended, reduces linearly to the peak negative pressure $p^{-}$ at a time equal to 25% of $t_{o f}$ , and then rises linearly to zero at time $t_{o f}$ after the end of the positive phase blast load. The effects of the dynamic pressure in the negative phase region usually may be neglected for analysis of structural elements where the negative phase loading is minimal or the rebound response is not critical.
